**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard my name spoken aloud, it was in a voice I didn’t recognize. My mother’s lips formed the syllables like a prayer, but the sound that came out was foreign—too sharp, too precise. She had chosen it carefully, she said, from a book of names she’d found in a secondhand shop. *"It means ‘light,’"* she told me, tracing the letters in the air. I was six years old, and I believed her.

But names are never just what they mean. They are the first thing people remember about you, the thing they cling to when the rest of you slips away. My name became a weight, then a brand, then a joke. *"Oh, you’re that girl,"* people would say, as if the name alone could sum me up. As if it could explain the way I held my breath in crowded rooms, as if it could account for the way my hands trembled when I wrote my own signature.

I tried to shed it. I wrote it backward in my notebooks, whispered it under my breath like a secret. But names, like ghosts, refuse to be exorcised. They linger in the margins of things—on receipts, on driver’s licenses, on the lips of strangers who mispronounce them just to see me correct them. Once, a man at a party laughed and said, *"You don’t look like a Light."* I wanted to tell him that names aren’t about looks. They’re about the way the world tries to pin you down.

I changed my name once. Not legally, not officially—just in my head. I called myself something softer, something that didn’t carry the echo of my mother’s voice or the sneers of classmates. But the old name clung to me like a second skin. It was in the way my teacher pronounced it wrong in front of the class. It was in the way my own reflection in the mirror didn’t match the name I’d given myself.

Names are promises, I think now. Promises about who you’ll be, who you’ll become. My mother’s name for me was a promise that I would be bright, that I would shine. But brightness isn’t always kind. Sometimes it burns.

I don’t know what my name means anymore. Maybe it doesn’t mean anything at all. Maybe it’s just a sound, a habit, a way for people to find me in a crowd. But I still hear it sometimes, in the silence between thoughts, in the way my fingers hover over the keyboard before I type it out.

And sometimes, when the world feels too heavy, I wonder if I could start over. If I could un-name myself and begin again, with something new, something that doesn’t carry the weight of all the things I’ve been called.

But names are like scars. They don’t go away. They just learn to fade.

---

**The Art of Forgetting**

Forgetting is an art, and I am its worst student.

I forget where I left my keys. I forget the names of people I’ve known for years. I forget the plot of a movie I just watched, the lyrics to a song I hummed all day. My brain is a sieve, a leaky faucet, a house with all the doors left ajar. People tell me I’m "distracted," but distraction is just the polite way of saying *I am not here*.

I try to compensate. I write things down. I set reminders. I repeat things aloud like a parrot, hoping the repetition will stick. But forgetting isn’t just about memory—it’s about presence. It’s about the way I can be in a room full of people and still feel like I’m watching myself from outside.

My mother used to say, *"You’re too soft, my love."* She meant it as a compliment. *"You forget things because you’re kind."* But kindness isn’t the reason I forget. Kindness is the reason I remember. I remember the way my grandmother’s hands shook when she held my face. I remember the exact moment my best friend told me she was leaving. I remember the taste of rain on pavement, the way my father’s laugh sounded like a door closing.

Forgetting is the thing I do when the remembering becomes too much.

I forget the names of my own children sometimes. Not their faces—never their faces—but the names that went with them. I forget what I was going to say mid-sentence, mid-breath. I forget how to tie my shoes, how to parallel park, how to breathe when the world feels like it’s pressing down on me.

People say, *"You’ll get better with age."* But age doesn’t fix forgetting. Age just adds more things to forget. It’s like trying to fill a bucket with holes. No matter how much you pour in, some of it always leaks out.

I dream of a world where forgetting is optional. Where I can choose to hold on to things, to keep them close like secrets. But the world doesn’t work that way. The world is a series of losses, a slow unraveling. And I am just another thread in its fabric, fraying at the edges.

So I forget. And I try not to mind.

---

**The House on the Hill**

The house on the hill was always there, watching.

It stood like a sentinel, its windows like hollow eyes, its roof sagging under the weight of decades. The neighbors called it *"the haunted house,"* though no one had ever seen a ghost. No one except me.

I was twelve when I first noticed it. I lived across the street, and every afternoon, I’d sit on my porch swing, watching the light shift across its peeling paint. The house had no curtains. No one ever came or went. No cars parked in the driveway. No mail sat on the porch.

One evening, as the sun bled into twilight, I saw a figure move inside. A shadow, really—a ripple in the glass. I squinted. It was a woman, standing in the kitchen, her back to the window. She was holding something small and white, something that glinted in the fading light.

I should have looked away. But I didn’t.

The next day, I asked my father about the house. *"That’s old Mrs. Holloway’s place,"* he said. *"She died years ago. The house is empty now."* I pressed him. *"What happened to her?"* He sighed. *"Nothing. She just… left."* That wasn’t an answer. Answers weren’t supposed to be that vague.

I started visiting the house.

At first, it was just to watch. Then, I began leaving things. A doll, half-buried in the overgrown bushes. A notebook, its pages blank. A single red rose, pressed between the cracks in the foundation. I didn’t know why. I just knew that the house needed something.

One night, I dreamed of her. Mrs. Holloway. She was standing in the doorway, her dress the color of old bones. *"You’ve been coming,"* she said. It wasn’t a question. *"I know."* She held out her hand. I reached for it, but when I woke up, my palm was empty.

The house changed after that.

The windows weren’t empty anymore. Sometimes, I saw faces in them—flickering, like candle flames. The door creaked open on its own. Once, I found a child’s boot print in the mud by the porch.

I told myself it was the wind. I told myself it was my imagination.

But then, one morning, I found a letter on my porch. It was addressed to me.

*"Dear [My Name],"* it read. *"You’ve been a good neighbor. Come inside when you’re ready."*

I burned it.

The house didn’t seem to mind.

Now, I don’t go near it. Not even to watch. Because sometimes, when I close my eyes, I can still see her standing there, waiting.

And I know she’s still watching.

---

**The Last Letter**

I found the letter in the attic, tucked between an old coat and a yellowed photograph of my grandfather. The envelope was brittle, the paper inside so thin it felt like it might dissolve if I breathed too hard.

*"My dearest [My Name],"*

I don’t remember writing this. I don’t remember ever writing anything to myself.

*"If you’re reading this, I’m already gone. Or maybe I never was here at all. Time is a funny thing. It bends. It breaks. It forgets. But letters, letters are different. They hold on. They wait."*

I traced the words with my fingertip. The ink was faded, but the handwriting was unmistakable—my own.

*"I’m writing this now because I don’t know if I’ll ever have the chance to say it to your face. Maybe you’ll find this years from now, when you’re old and gray and the world feels like it’s crumbling around you. Or maybe you’ll find it today, and it will feel like a punch to the gut."*

I stopped reading. My hands were shaking.

*"I love you. Not in the way people say they love things—the way they love their coffee, or their favorite song, or the way the sun looks over the ocean. I love you in the way that things break. In the way that some doors only open from the inside. In the way that some loves are so deep they become part of you, like the bones."*

I pressed my palm to my chest. There was a hollow there, a space that had been left empty.

*"You were always my favorite kind of storm. The kind that comes without warning, that shakes the world until it remembers how to tremble. I wanted to tell you that. I wanted to tell you that you were enough. That you were allowed to be loud and messy and impossible. That I would always be here, even when you couldn’t see me."*

I turned the letter over. On the back, in smaller, shakier script, were two words:

*"Goodbye."*

I didn’t cry. I didn’t scream. I just sat there, holding the letter like it was the last thing I’d ever touch.

Because it was.

Because I had written it.

And I had forgotten.

---

**The Sound of Silence**

Silence isn’t the absence of sound. It’s the space between the things that aren’t said.

I learned this the hard way.

My father was a man of few words. Not because he was quiet, but because he knew the weight of them. He could fill a room with his presence, but his voice was a rare thing. I remember sitting at the kitchen table, watching him pour coffee, listening to the clink of the spoon against the mug. The only sound in the house was the hum of the refrigerator and the distant murmur of the street.

One night, when I was ten, I asked him, *"Dad, why don’t you talk more?"*

He didn’t look up from his plate. *"Because some things don’t need words."*

I didn’t understand then. I thought silence was failure. I thought it meant he didn’t care.

But silence is a language all its own.

I learned it from my mother. She was the one who taught me how to listen. How to read between the lines of a furrowed brow, the way her hands clenched when she was angry, the way her breath hitched when she was afraid. She didn’t need to say it. I just had to *see*.

My brother, on the other hand, was the opposite. He was a storm of words, a whirlwind of laughter and curses and half-formed thoughts. He talked so much that sometimes I forgot he was even there. But when he was quiet, it was like the world held its breath.

I used to think silence was a punishment. That if I just talked enough, if I filled the air with enough noise, I could drown out the things I didn’t want to hear.

But silence isn’t a punishment. It’s a choice.

It’s the choice to let the words breathe. To let the spaces between them matter.

I learned this the day my mother died.

The funeral was silent. Not because no one spoke, but because the words were too heavy to carry. We stood in the church, surrounded by the weight of absence, and no one said a thing. And in that silence, I understood.

Silence isn’t the absence of sound. It’s the space where the soul finds its voice.

---

**The Thing About Time**

Time is a liar.

It tells you that you’ll have forever. That the sun will always rise. That the people you love will always be there.

But time doesn’t lie. It just *is*.

I used to think time was a river. Smooth, endless, flowing in one direction. But rivers don’t remember. They don’t care. They just keep going, indifferent to the things they leave behind.

Time is more like a knife.

It cuts. It carves. It leaves scars.

I remember the first time I realized time was real. I was eight years old, sitting on the floor of my bedroom, watching my father shave. The razor glinted in the light, and for a second, I thought it was a sword. *"Time is like this,"* he said, pressing the blade to his cheek. *"It’s sharp. It’s precise. And if you’re not careful, it’ll cut you."*

I didn’t understand then. I thought he was talking about the razor.

But he wasn’t.

Time doesn’t just pass. It *takes*. It takes the youth from your skin. It takes the fire from your eyes. It takes the people you love until there’s nothing left but echoes.

I used to fight it. I tried to freeze time. I memorized every detail of every day, like a child trying to hold onto a sandcastle before the tide comes in. But time doesn’t care about your memories. It doesn’t care about your regrets. It just keeps moving.

Now, I’ve learned to let it.

I let it take the things that don’t matter. The small things—the lost keys, the forgotten names, the way I used to hum a song I can’t remember now. But I hold onto the big things. The love. The laughter. The way my mother’s laugh still sounds like sunlight.

Time is a thief. But it’s also a gift.

Because without it, we wouldn’t know what we’re missing.

---

**The Weight of a Name (Revisited)**

I changed my name again.

This time, it was legal. This time, it was *mine*.

I chose something soft. Something that didn’t carry the weight of my past. Something that didn’t make people pause when they heard it.

But names are like ghosts. They don’t stay buried.

The first time someone called me by my old name, I almost flinched. The second time, I laughed. The third time, I didn’t even look up.

Because names aren’t just words. They’re identities. They’re histories. They’re the things that define us, even when we try to leave them behind.

I still hear my mother’s voice sometimes, whispering my old name like a prayer. I still see the way people’s eyes flicker when they realize they’ve mispronounced it. But I don’t mind anymore.

Because names are just names.

And I’m not just a name.

I’m a person. A woman. A daughter. A sister. A lover. A survivor.

And none of those things are defined by the sound of my name.

---

**The End (Or Maybe Just the Beginning)**

I don’t know what comes next.

But I know this: words are like seeds. They take root in the dark, and if you water them right, they grow into something beautiful.

So I’ll keep writing. I’ll keep speaking. I’ll keep being.

Because silence isn’t the absence of sound. It’s just the space between the things that matter.

And I’m not going to let that space be too big.

---
